name: Speed conversion
seoTitle: Speed conversion Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Speed conversion: work out miles per hour from the feet per second. A free conversion calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Speed conversion calculator is a free, no-sign-up conversion tool. Fill in the 1 field it asks for and it works out miles per hour straight away, with the formula shown underneath. That makes it useful for a recipe, a shopping list, a travel plan or a form that asks for a unit you do not use. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Speed conversion calculator work?
sections.html:
The Speed conversion calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports miles per hour in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the feet per second.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A measured quantity, entered by default in feet per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Speed conversion calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Miles per hour=feet per second
Miles per hour=yards per second
Miles per hour=more imperial ÷ US units
Miles per hour=kilometers per hour
Miles per hour=meters per second
Miles per hour=kilometers per second

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Minutes per mile and seconds per mile = 10 sec/mile. Working through the relationship above gives Miles per hour = 579.3638 mph, Feet per second = 579.3638 ft/s, Yards per second = 579.3638 yd/s and More imperial/US units = 579.3638 mi/s.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Miles per hour = 579.3638 mph, Feet per second = 579.3638 ft/s, Yards per second = 579.3638 yd/s and More imperial/US units = 579.3638 mi/s should be roughly the size you expected from Minutes per mile and seconds per mile = 10 sec/mile.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Speed, opening in miles per hour
  • Speed, opening in feet per second
  • Speed, opening in yards per second
  • Speed, opening in miles per second
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per hour
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per second
  • Speed, opening in centimeters per second

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Speed conversion calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a product listing against the measurements you work with
  • Filling in a form that asks for imperial or metric values
  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the feet per second — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Speed conversion calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns miles per hour, derived from the feet per second. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Speed conversion calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the feet per second, which is 1 field in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter miles per hour in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Miles per hour opens in miles per hour and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Miles per hour = 579.3638 mph. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Speed conversion calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
